ECOLOGY

Discuss the following questions: I. What comes to mind when you hear the word ‘ecosystem’? II. Can you name one example of natural ecosystem? III. How do you think living things in an ecosystem are connected? IV. What role do you think plants play in an ecosystem? V. Why might studying ecosystems be important for understanding the environment?
4.1.1 CONCEPT OF ECOLOGY

All the things of the world are classified into two major groups namely living and non-living things. The living things includes all types of life and is known as biotic component while nonliving things includes soil, water, air, light, etc. and is known as abiotic components.
The inter-relationship between biotic and abiotic components as well as the relationship among the individuals of the biotic component is called ecology.

The word ecology (Greek; oikos-household, logos-study) was coined by Hanns Reiter (1885). Literally ecology means the study of organism at home. The ‘home’ includes the entire physical environment as well as other organisms that are there. Thus, ecology is the branch of Biology that studies the interrelationships between organisms and their environment.
Ecology is divided into two groups:
1. Autoecology: It is a study of relationship between individual species or its population and its environment.

2. Synecology: It is a study of relationship between the individual of different species or its population and its environment. It is concerned with the structure, nature, development and causes of distribution of population of different species.
4.1.2 ECOLOGICAL FACTORS

Any factor, abiotic or biotic, that influences the living beings are called as ecological factors or environmental factors. These factors either singly or in combination influence or determine the presence or absence, vigour or weakness and relative success or failure of various plant communities in a particular habitat. Ecological factors are classified into two groups:

1. Abiotic Factors: The non-living things of the environment are known as abiotic factors. The abiotic factors that influence the living beings are grouped into three main group: climatic factors, topographic factor and Edaphic factor.
a. Climatic factors : It includes:

i. Sunlight – It plays the most important role in an ecosystem. It is the primary source of energy for all living organisms in an ecosystem. It is necessary for photosynthesis, chlorophyll formation, stomatal movement, transpiration, etc in plant and locomotion, migration of organisms, pigmentation, metabolism, vision etc. in animal. ii. Temperature – It is the another most important factors of an ecosystem. It plays role in transpiration, respiration, photosynthesis, seed germination, flowering, growth and development etc. in plant and reproduction, colouration, hibernation, aestivation, thermal migration, etc. in animal. iii. Pressure – The atmospheric pressure varies at different place. The vegetation types and life also varies accordingly and thus the ecosystems are different at different places. iv. Rainfall – The vegetation types and its density depend on the quantity of rainfall. Heavy throughout the year favours evergreen forest while low rainfall retards the growth the plant and favours the xerophytic vegetation. v. Humidity – The amount of water vapour in the atmosphere is humidity. It directly influences the rate of photosynthesis, transpiration, absorption of water etc. b. Topographic factors: It mainly concerned with surface features of the Earth and includes altitude, latitude, slope, steepness etc. The variation in these factors causes the variation in climatic factors.
c. Edaphic factors: It concerned with soil factors. It includes texture, organism, temperature, pH, air, water etc of soil.
2. Biotic factors:

The living things of the environment are known as biotic factors. The biotic factor includes all types of life forms and categorized in three groups on the basis of food relationship i.e. producer, consumer and decomposer.
